passage:
Saturday, 10 pm.

Dad moved out today. His bags were by the door at nine and the car left before lunch. Mum kept saying "we're all fine" in a bright voice. I said I was fine too. I wasn't. I went to the bathroom, turned on the tap and cried until my head ached.

Still set my alarm. Still did homework. It helps to have things that stay the same.

Told Vandana at lunch. She didn't say anything smart, just sat next to me on the steps and let me cry a bit more. She's going to come over tomorrow.

I keep thinking of our old Sundays. I miss a family that turns out not to have been there. It's my loss too.

Payal

qa.q: What time were Dad's bags by the door?
qa.a: His bags were by the door at nine.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling when saying "fine" and then going to the bathroom to cry?
qa.a: Payal was grieving and sad, and said "fine" to match Mum's bright voice.

qa.q: What did Payal do that helps with coping?
qa.a: Payal cried instead of holding it in, kept the alarm and homework routine, and told Vandana about it.

qa.q: What might Vandana have been thinking as she sat on the steps without saying anything?
qa.a: Perhaps that there were no right words and that staying close mattered more than advice, so she simply sat with Payal and let the crying happen. 🤍

grounding: Shows a teen mourning the family they thought they had, letting the tears come, keeping routines and confiding in a friend.

passage:
Saturday
Papa took the last of his books to the new flat today. The shelf in the hall looks like a mouth with missing teeth. I kept thinking of Sunday mornings when the three of us made dosas and fought over the crispy ones. That family is gone, and I didn't get a vote.
I cried in the shower so nobody would hear. Then I thought, why hide? So I stuck a note on my mirror: Ritu, you're allowed to cry.
I still went to badminton. I still did the maths worksheet. Having something normal helps.
At lunch on Friday Vijay just sat with me and shared his chips without saying anything clever. Monday I'm going to see Ms Farida, the school counsellor. I don't want to keep saying "I'm fine" to everyone. It isn't true.

qa.q: What did Papa take to the new flat on Saturday?
What does Ritu's note on the mirror suggest about Ritu's feelings?
qa.a: It shows Ritu is grieving the family that used to be and has decided that crying is allowed instead of hiding the sadness.

qa.q: Which choices are helping Ritu cope?
qa.a: Ritu keeps routines like badminton and homework, lets the tears come, accepts Vijay's quiet company and has planned to see the school counsellor.

qa.q: How might Vijay see Ritu at lunch?
qa.a: Vijay seems to sense Ritu is hurting and chooses to simply stay close, sharing his chips, rather than trying to fix things with words.

grounding: A teen mourns the family that used to be as the parents separate, allows tears, keeps routines and turns to a friend and a counsellor.

passage:
Tejas: u ok? u left maths without ur bag
Disha: yeah fine
Tejas: disha
Disha: ok not fine
Disha: they signed the papers today. mum is keeping the flat, dad is moving to Nashik
Disha: i keep thinking about our old holidays and how that's just over now
Tejas: that's a real loss. you're allowed to be sad about it
Disha: i've been pretending all week so mum doesn't cry more
Tejas: you don't have to hold everyone up. can you tell her how you feel?
Disha: maybe
Tejas: i'll bring ur bag tomorrow. still coming to practice?
Disha: yeah. i need something normal
Disha: mum just knocked. she saw my face
Disha: i told her i'm not okay. she's sitting on my bed now. she's crying too but she's holding my hand
Tejas: good. text me later if u want

qa.q: Why had Disha been pretending to be fine all week?
qa.a: Disha was grieving but felt responsible for protecting Mum from more pain, so Disha hid the sadness to keep things calm.

qa.q: How could a friend like Tejas keep supporting Disha?
qa.a: Keep checking in, bring the bag, protect the routine of practice and keep encouraging Disha to share feelings with Mum or another trusted adult.

qa.q: What is it like for Mum when she sees Disha's face?
qa.a: She seems moved and sad; she stops to sit on the bed, cries too and holds Disha's hand, showing she wants to share the grief rather than be protected.

grounding: A teen grieving a parents' divorce stops pretending to be fine, keeps a routine and opens up to a friend and to Mum.
